headline: Carter bans grain sales to the Soviet Union
text: On 4 January President Carter announced a grain embargo against the Soviet Union, days after Soviet troops entered Afghanistan. He wants to punish Moscow without sending soldiers. The hostages in Tehran are still held, and the president faces an election in November.

headline: Gold touches 843 dollars and silver 49.45, both records
text: Silver reached a record 49.45 dollars an ounce on 18 January, and the London gold fixing touched 843 on the 21st. Savers fear inflation and war and want metal that cannot be printed. Silver's rise is helped by the Hunt brothers of Texas, who by late 1979 controlled about 195 million ounces. Prices this high can fall fast.

headline: Chrysler gets its 1.5 billion dollar lifeline
text: President Carter signed a law on 7 January that guarantees up to 1.5 billion dollars of loans to the car maker Chrysler, which Congress passed in December. In return Chrysler must cut costs, sell assets and win pay concessions from its workers. It is the largest government rescue of a private company so far.

headline: Six Americans slip out of Tehran with Canadian passports
text: On 27 January six American diplomats, who had been hiding in Tehran, flew out of Iran posing as Canadians, with Canadian passports. It is the one piece of good news in the hostage crisis. The other 50-odd Americans remain in captivity.

headline: Steelers win Super Bowl XIV, and a new comic strip starts
text: The Pittsburgh Steelers beat the Los Angeles Rams 31 to 19 on 20 January to win Super Bowl XIV. On 1 January a new newspaper comic strip, The Far Side, made its debut.

headline: Miracle on Ice: American students beat the Soviet hockey team
text: At the Winter Olympics in Lake Placid, which opened on 13 February, the US ice hockey team beat the Soviet Union on the 22nd. In a winter of hostages and Afghanistan, Americans have been waiting for a win over the Soviets.

headline: Iran gets its first president, the hostages stay
text: Abolhassan Banisadr was sworn in on 4 February as Iran's first president. The students who hold the US embassy are still holding the Americans, three months after the seizure.

headline: FBI agents posing as Arab sheikhs offered bribes to Congressmen
text: On 3 February newspapers revealed Abscam, an FBI sting in which agents posed as rich Arab sheikhs and offered money to members of Congress in return for favours. Several lawmakers are reported to be under investigation. Who, if anyone, will be charged is not yet known.

headline: Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett's holding company, is now available to you
text: Berkshire Hathaway from Omaha began as a textile maker and now owns insurers, See's Candies and the Buffalo Evening News, and holds 5.7 million shares of the insurer GEICO. Buffett reported that book value per share rose from 19.46 dollars in 1964 to 335.85 at the end of 1979. It ploughs its profits back into the business instead of paying them out, and has never split its share, so one is expensive.

headline: Intel, the maker of the computer chip, is now available to you
text: Intel, a California company, built the first commercial microprocessor, a whole computer processor on one chip, in 1971, and its memory chip was the bestseller in the world by 1972. In 1978 it brought out the 8086, a more powerful 16-bit chip. Buy it if you think small computers will spread, and know that memory chips are a tough business.

headline: Carter clamps down on credit in the fight against inflation
text: On 14 March Carter announced the first credit controls since the Second World War. The Federal Reserve limited the growth of lending and put restrictions on credit cards and instalment loans. The move came with inflation and short-term interest rates both near 18 percent in early 1980.

headline: Silver Thursday: silver crashes from 50 dollars to 10.80
text: The silver bubble burst on 27 March. Silver fell to 10.80 dollars an ounce after the Hunt brothers could no longer pay for their huge, borrowed position. One broker alone was owed some 122 million dollars it could not collect. Thirteen banks lent 1.1 billion dollars to a Hunt company to avoid a wider collapse.

headline: Carter announces a US boycott of the Moscow Olympics
text: On 21 March President Carter said that American athletes will not go to the Summer Olympics in Moscow in July. It is his answer to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. Other countries must decide whether to follow.

headline: Sandoz's anti-rejection drug is used in a liver transplant
text: Doctors in Pittsburgh used Sandoz's new drug, cyclosporin, in a liver transplant on 9 March. Sandoz scientists found its power to damp the body's immune system in January 1972 in a fungus from Norwegian soil, and Cambridge doctors have shown it helps kidney transplants survive. It is still in trials.

headline: McDonald's tests Chicken McNuggets in Knoxville
text: McDonald's began a test of Chicken McNuggets, a recipe by its first executive chef, Rene Arend, in Knoxville, Tennessee, this March. Early sales are so strong that chicken is running short. The test runs in six restaurants around Knoxville, at 1.10 dollars for five pieces.

headline: America breaks off relations with Iran
text: On 7 April the US cut diplomatic ties with Iran and imposed sanctions, five months after the embassy was seized. The 50-odd hostages are still there.

headline: Rescue attempt in Iran fails, eight US soldiers dead
text: On 24 and 25 April a secret US attempt to free the hostages, Operation Eagle Claw, ended in the Iranian desert when a helicopter hit a transport plane. Eight American servicemen died. Secretary of State Cyrus Vance resigned in protest at the plan.

headline: Zimbabwe becomes independent with Robert Mugabe as prime minister
text: The former British colony of Rhodesia became independent as Zimbabwe on 18 April. Robert Mugabe, who won the election in March, leads the first government. It ends years of civil war.

headline: Wal-Mart sells a billion dollars in a year, with 276 stores
text: Wal-Mart, the discount store chain, passed one billion dollars of sales in its business year that ended on 31 January, and has 276 stores in 11 states. Founder Sam Walton keeps profit margins lower than his rivals and makes up for it with volume.

headline: Kramer vs. Kramer wins the Oscars
text: The 52nd Academy Awards on 14 April went to Kramer vs. Kramer, which won both Best Picture and Best Director.

headline: Mount St. Helens erupts
text: The volcano in Washington State blew up on 18 May. Fifty-seven people died and the damage was put at 3 billion dollars.

headline: Smallpox is declared gone from the Earth, and Marshal Tito dies
text: On 8 May the World Health Organization certified that smallpox, a deadly disease, has been wiped out across the world. Four days earlier Yugoslavia's President Josip Broz Tito died; his state funeral was the largest in history.

headline: The Empire Strikes Back opens, and Pac-Man arrives in Japan
text: The Empire Strikes Back, the sequel to Star Wars, opened in cinemas on 21 May. The next day the arcade game Pac-Man went on sale in Japan.

headline: Sony brings the Walkman to America
text: Sony's pocket cassette player, launched in Japan on 1 July 1979 at about 33,000 yen, reached the US in June under names such as Soundabout. Sony expected 5,000 sales a month, yet sold over 30,000 in the first two months in Japan. Young people want music they can carry around.

headline: CNN starts the world's first 24-hour news channel
text: On 1 June the Cable News Network officially launched as the first 24-hour news channel. News on television no longer has to wait for the evening bulletin.

headline: Young men must register for the draft again
text: On 27 June Carter signed an order requiring 19 and 20 year-old men to register for military service, a response to Afghanistan. Registering is not the same as being drafted, but it makes a draft possible again.

headline: Credit controls end as unemployment rises and interest rates fall
text: On 3 July the Federal Reserve announced the end of the credit controls from March, which it had already eased in May. The share of Americans without a job jumped to 7.8 percent this spring, and the prime rate, the rate banks charge their best customers, has fallen to 11 percent. Whether the worst is over, nobody can say.

headline: Republicans nominate Ronald Reagan for president
text: On 16 July the Republican convention in Detroit chose Ronald Reagan, former governor of California, to challenge Carter in November.

headline: Moscow Olympics start with a Western boycott; the exiled Shah dies
text: The Summer Olympics opened in Moscow on 19 July with many Western countries staying away over Afghanistan. A week later, on 27 July, the Shah of Iran, whom the hostage-takers want handed over, died of cancer in Cairo.

headline: Miller beer has taken Philip Morris from seventh to second place
text: Philip Morris bought Miller Brewing in 1970 when it was the seventh-largest US brewer. Helped by Miller Lite, it had climbed to second place by 1977, behind only Anheuser-Busch. The company is best known for Marlboro, the world's best-selling cigarette brand since 1972.

headline: Polish shipyard workers strike and win a free trade union
text: Strikes began in Lublin in July, and in August Lech Walesa led the strikes at the Gdansk shipyard. On 31 August the government signed the Gdansk Agreement, which opens the way to the first free trade union in the communist bloc.

headline: Democrats renominate Carter
text: President Carter beat Senator Ted Kennedy at the Democratic convention on 14 August. He now has to face Ronald Reagan in November, with the hostages still in Iran.

headline: Hurricane Allen batters Haiti and Texas
text: Hurricane Allen killed over 200 people in Haiti on 4 August as a Category 5 storm, and hit southeastern Texas on the 10th as a Category 3.

headline: Bomb in Bologna station kills 85
text: A bomb in the railway station of Bologna, Italy, killed 85 people and wounded over 200 on 2 August.

headline: Iraq attacks Iran, oil prices on edge
text: Iraq attacked Iran on 22 September. The fighting disrupts oil production in the region and makes it harder for OPEC, which already has no common price, to hold its members together.

headline: The world's longest road tunnel opens through the Alps
text: The Gotthard Road Tunnel opened on 5 September. At 16.9 kilometres it is the longest road tunnel in the world and links Goeschenen in Uri with Airolo in Ticino in about 13 minutes, all year round.

headline: Intel, with DEC and Xerox, publishes a standard to link computers
text: On 30 September Intel, Digital Equipment and Xerox published the DIX Ethernet standard, a way of connecting computers by cable at 10 megabits a second. The three companies hope that other makers will adopt it.

headline: Turkey's army takes power
text: On 12 September the Turkish army under General Kenan Evren seized power in a coup.

headline: Nestle brings a German in to run the whole group
text: Helmut Maucher moved from Frankfurt to Nestle's headquarters in Switzerland on 1 October as general director of the whole group and member of the executive committee. He joined Nestle aged 19 at a German dairy it bought, and has run its German business since 1975. The Swiss food group also owns Alcon, bought in 1977 for 280 million dollars.

headline: Reagan pulls ahead after the debate with Carter
text: Carter and Reagan met on television in Cleveland on 28 October, a week before the vote. Reagan did well, and his poll numbers jumped.

headline: Poland officially recognises Solidarity
text: On 31 October the Polish government recognised the free trade union Solidarity.

headline: Philadelphia Phillies win the World Series for the first time
text: The Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals four games to two on 21 October, the first World Series win in the club's history.

headline: Reagan beats Carter in a landslide
text: Ronald Reagan won the presidency on 4 November with 489 electoral votes to 49 and about 51 percent of the vote to Carter's 41. He carried 44 states. Voters were asked whether they were better off than four years ago, and most said no.

headline: Dow climbs back above 1000 after the election
text: Shares jumped after the election: on the day after the vote, trading on the New York Stock Exchange set a record of 84 million shares. About two weeks after the election the Dow Jones average moved above 1,000 for the first time since 1976.

headline: Who shot J.R.? A whole country wants to know
text: The question "Who shot J.R.?", about a character in the TV series Dallas, became a national obsession. The episode that answered it was shown on 21 November.

headline: Earthquake in southern Italy kills thousands
text: A 6.9 magnitude earthquake hit Irpinia in southern Italy on 23 November and killed at least 2,483 people.

headline: Apple Computer, maker of the Apple II, is now available to you
text: Apple Computer went public on 12 December: 4.6 million shares at 22 dollars raised over 100 million, the biggest offering since Ford in 1956, and by the close they traded at 29. It makes personal computers for home and office; sales were 118 million dollars in 1980. The founders, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, and about 300 others became millionaires.

headline: John Lennon shot dead outside his New York home
text: Former Beatle John Lennon was shot and killed on 8 December outside the Dakota building in New York by Mark David Chapman.

headline: Banks raise the prime rate to a record 21.5 percent
text: In mid-December major US banks lifted the prime rate, what they charge their best customers, from 20 to a record 21 percent, and on 19 December it reached 21.5 percent. In July it was 11 percent. Mortgages and business loans cost more than ever, and many expect a recession early next year.

headline: Dow ends the year at 964, up 15 percent despite a December dip
text: The Dow Jones average closed 1980 at 963.99, a gain of 14.9 percent, after sinking to 911 in December from the post-election high above 1,000. Shares ended the year higher despite interest rates at record highs.

headline: General Electric chooses Jack Welch, 45, as its next chairman
text: General Electric announced in December that Jack Welch will succeed chairman Reginald Jones next year. At 45 he is young for the job. GE makes everything from jet engines to light bulbs and Jones, whom a US magazine named the most influential man in business this year, is stepping down after nine years.

headline: Schlumberger's value ranks fourth in the world behind IBM, AT&T and Exxon
text: The oil boom has made Schlumberger, a services company for oil drillers with pumping and drilling businesses, one of the most valuable companies in the world: fourth by market value this year, behind only IBM, AT&T and Exxon. In 1979 it also paid 425 million dollars for Fairchild Camera and Instrument, a US electronics group.
